lesson.title: Building a Guarantee on Top of an Unreliable Network
lesson.summary: Reliable delivery is the set of mechanisms, sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and retransmission, that a connection oriented protocol like TCP uses to guarantee that data arrives complete and in order despite running over a network layer that only offers best effort delivery.
lesson.body:
Reliable delivery is what a connection oriented protocol builds on top of the connection state it establishes during its handshake. Where best effort delivery, covered just before this, makes no promises about loss, duplication, or ordering, reliable delivery makes a strong promise: data will arrive complete and in the order it was sent, or the sender will be able to tell that something went wrong. TCP is the internet's primary example of a reliable delivery protocol, and understanding how it achieves this is a natural extension of understanding connection oriented service, since the connection state a handshake establishes is exactly the bookkeeping reliability requires.

The mechanisms are a handful of coordinated ideas working together. Every byte of data in a TCP connection is assigned a sequence number, so the receiver always knows exactly where a given segment fits in the overall stream. The receiver sends acknowledgments back to the sender confirming how much data it has successfully received in order. A checksum in each segment lets the receiver detect corruption introduced in transit. If the sender does not receive an acknowledgment within an expected window of time, a retransmission timer expires and the sender resends the data, assuming it may have been lost. The receiver also buffers data that arrives out of order, holding it until the missing pieces show up so the completed stream can be delivered to the application in the correct order despite the network reordering it along the way.

It is important to see that reliable delivery is achieved entirely by the endpoints, not by the network layer underneath, which is precisely the end to end principle in action: IP continues to offer only best effort delivery for every individual packet that makes up a TCP connection, and TCP compensates for that unreliability using nothing but state held at the two communicating hosts. Every guarantee TCP offers is a guarantee about what the endpoints do with an unreliable network, not a change to the network itself.

A concrete worked example shows the mechanism clearly. Suppose a sender transmits five TCP segments carrying sequence numbers 1 through 5 in order, and segment 3 is lost somewhere in the network. The receiver gets segments 1, 2, 4, and 5, notices a gap where 3 should be, and continues acknowledging only up through the end of segment 2, since that is the last point up to which it has a complete, in order stream. The sender, seeing repeated acknowledgments that are not advancing past segment 2, or alternatively seeing its retransmission timer for segment 3 expire, resends segment 3. Once the receiver gets the retransmitted segment 3, it now has all five segments, reassembles them in correct order using their sequence numbers, and delivers the complete, correctly ordered stream up to the application, which never sees any evidence that a loss or reordering happened at all.

This is also why reliable delivery has a cost that best effort delivery does not: buffering out of order data, tracking acknowledgments, and waiting for retransmission timers all add latency and consume memory at the endpoints. That cost is exactly why not every application chooses reliable delivery, and why connectionless, best effort transport remains the right choice for applications like live video where a late retransmission is worse than no retransmission at all.
